one_liner: Threaded cv::Mat kernels that replace OpenCV 4.14 resize (cubic downscale, integer INTER_AREA), transform and general-exponent pow.
what_it_does: fastcv is a static library of about 30 functions in namespace fastcv, each a one-file replacement for one OpenCV call with the same cv::Mat in/out shape: resizeCubic8u(src, dst, dsize), resizeAreaInt8u(src, dst, factor), transform32f(src, dst, m) and pow32f(src, dst, power) are the colour-and-resampling ones. It is not a drop-in library swap: you call fastcv:: instead of cv:: per site, and the kernels cover narrow cases (8UC1/8UC3 for resize, integer factors that divide the image for area, CV_32FC1 for pow, 32F with up to 4 channels for transform). It ships with the author's patched OpenCV 4.14.0 build scripts, a C API (fastcv_c.h) and a Rust FFI crate, all from a 6-commit, 0-star repository.
how_it_is_fast: Mostly parallelism: every kernel runs a plain cv::parallel_for_ over rows with no stripe hint, while OpenCV 4.14.0 runs cv::transform and the general cv::pow single-threaded (NAryMatIterator) and runs resize with nstripes = dst.total()/65536. That OpenCV heuristic gives about 2 stripes for a 480x270 INTER_AREA x4 output, about 8 for a 960x540 cubic downscale and about 32 for a 1920x1080 upscale (derived from OpenCV's resize.cpp), which fits fastcv winning on downscale and losing on upscale. resizeCubic8u also does a two-phase separable pass (horizontal 11-bit fixed-point into an int buffer, with an AVX-512 32-bit gather of 4 taps for C1 interior pixels, then a float SIMD vertical pass), so each source row is filtered once. pow32f replaces OpenCV's SIMD log32f/exp32f plus its zero/negative fix-up loop with fused exp2(p*log2(x)) polynomials (atanh series for log2, degree-6 Taylor for exp2).
when_to_use: You already link OpenCV and do 8UC1/8UC3 INTER_CUBIC downscaling of 1080p-class frames on a many-core x86 box: the author's corrected figure is 1.5-1.9x with bit-exact output.
Integer-factor INTER_AREA decimation by 4 (or 3, 5, ...) on 8UC1/8UC3 where OpenCV's area-fast path only gets a couple of threads; x4 measured 18.7x (C1) and 3.5x (C3) with +/-1 differences.
Per-pixel 3-in/4-out float colour transforms (cv::transform with a 4x4 matrix on 32FC3), where OpenCV falls back to a single-threaded scalar loop.
Gamma curves on strictly positive CV_32FC1 data (for example after adding an epsilon), when about 1e-5 relative error is acceptable.
As a reference for how much of OpenCV's latency on a 32-thread CPU is threading policy rather than arithmetic.
when_not_to_use: Upscaling with INTER_CUBIC: the author's own log measures fastcv at 0.7-0.9x of OpenCV (slower) and says to keep cv::resize there.
INTER_AREA by 2: OpenCV's SIMD 2x2 path is faster (README and header both say use cv::resize for x2).
pow on data that can contain 0, negative values, NaN/Inf or results outside the float exponent range: pow32f returns garbage there, while cv::pow returns 0/inf/NaN.

Single-core, latency-bound or already-parallel pipelines (or calls from inside another cv::parallel_for_, where the nested loop runs serially): the speedups come largely from using all 32 threads of a Ryzen 9 9950X3D.
Production use that needs maintenance or review: 0 stars, no issues or third-party reports, one v1.0.0 release, comments and logs in Russian, and the README's headline cubic 4.1x is stale.

integration.form: static lib (libfastcv.a via scripts/build-fastcv.sh); single kernels can also be copied as one .cpp each
integration.dependencies: OpenCV core headers and library (built and tested against the repo's OpenCV 4.14.0 linux-dispatch install); the library build also passes -I/usr/include/openblas, and other kernels need OpenBLAS and FFTW (-lopenblas -lfftw3f -lfftw3f_threads); the four resampling/colour kernels need only opencv_core
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (README badge); g++ with -O3 -march=native (version not documented); OpenCV 4.x function-style universal intrinsics (v_add/v_mul/v_muladd)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 tested (Zen 5, AVX-512 + VBMI); resizeCubic8u's gather path needs AVX-512F at compile time and otherwise falls back to scalar; Windows MinGW and aarch64 builds are documented but not verified
integration.thread_safety: not documented; by code reading resizeCubic8u, resizeAreaInt8u, transform32f and pow32f keep no shared state and are reentrant, and they use OpenCV's thread pool (cv::setNumThreads applies)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same cv::Mat arguments, but you call fastcv:: per site and each kernel covers a subset of cv:: cases (no interpolation flag, no x2 area win, positive-only pow, no in-place resize)

gotchas: pow32f's x <= 0 mask is computed and discarded, and exp2 has no range clamp: zero inputs (black pixels in a gamma curve) give garbage instead of 0, and the repo's own test adds +0.001 to the image to avoid it.

cv::pow's general-exponent baseline in OpenCV 4.14.0 is vectorized (hal::log32f/exp32f in blocks, single-threaded), not scalar powf as the fastcv source comment says; the 19-22x is 32 threads plus cheaper polynomials, against a baseline that also does the zero/negative handling fastcv skips.

resizeAreaInt8u rounds ties up with (sum+8)>>4, while OpenCV's area-fast loop for x4 does saturate_cast(sum*(1/16.f)), which rounds half to even; by code reading about 1 in 32 output values should differ by 1 on uniform random input, more than the README's 0.2%, and the regression test's bound (img3.total()*3/100 = 62,208 of 388,800 output values) is far looser than its '<1% px' label. Its header comment promises SIMD, but the code is plain scalar loops left to the compiler.

The resize kernels call dst.create() before reading src and keep no copy of the src header, so passing the same Mat as src and dst breaks; resizeCubic8u also allocates a fresh sh x dw*cn int32 buffer every call (about 12 MB for 1080p C3 to 960x540). resizeCubic8u and transform32f have no regression tests, and transform32f's SIMD 3x3 path (FMA chain in a different order from OpenCV's v_matmuladd) was never benchmarked or checked for bit-exactness.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over KLERP, CompV or FlyCV when you want to keep cv::Mat and OpenCV's exact cubic coefficients and only fix the specific OpenCV calls that leave cores idle (cubic downscale, area x4, 3-to-4-channel transform); pick fast_image_resize or stb-image-resize-opt for a standalone, maintained resizer with many filters and published per-case results.
verified_claims_summary: The author measured on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D (32 threads, Arch Linux) against OpenCV 4.14.0 built from source with IPP off and TBB at default threads, using 1080p random images and 20-50 timed runs: cubic downscale 1.5-1.9x bit-exact (upscale 0.7-0.9x, slower), INTER_AREA x4 18.7x C1 and 3.5x C3, transform 32FC3 with a 4x4 matrix 10.7x, pow 19-22x on inputs in [0.01, 10]. No result files back these numbers, and every baseline except upscale cubic runs on far fewer threads than fastcv.
status_note: Created September 2026 (6 commits, v1.0.0 on 2026-09-08, last commit 2026-09-10, 0 stars, no issues); Apache-2.0 and the resampling kernels are single files depending only on opencv_core, so they are easy to vendor, but treat them as unreviewed.
